Front:
Reverse osmosis primarily removes:
a. Dissolved salts and many dissolved organics
b. Only suspended solids
c. Only bacteria
d. Only gases
Back: Answer: a. Dissolved salts and many dissolved organics

Front:
The “permeate” stream in an RO system is:
a. The treated, low-salinity water that has passed through the membranes
b. The concentrated reject stream
c. The feed entering the RO skid
d. The backwash water
Back: Answer: a. The treated, low-salinity water that has passed through the membranes

Front:
The “concentrate” or “brine” stream is:
a. The high-salt reject from RO membranes
b. The finished water
c. The MF filtrate
d. The chemical waste
Back: Answer: a. The high-salt reject from RO membranes

Front:
Recovery in an RO train is typically limited by:
a. Scaling and concentration of sparingly soluble salts
b. Membrane color
c. Permeate tank size only
d. Chlorine residual
Back: Answer: a. Scaling and concentration of sparingly soluble salts

Front:
An increase in RO differential pressure (Delta P) usually indicates:
a. Fouling or plugging of the RO elements
b. Membrane oxidation
c. Loss of salt rejection
d. Lower feed TDS
Back: Answer: a. Fouling or plugging of the RO elements

Front:
Loss of salt rejection with normal differential pressure (Delta P) often indicates:
a. Membrane damage or chemical attack
b. Colloidal fouling
c. Air entrainment
d. Low feed temperature
Back: Answer: a. Membrane damage or chemical attack

Front:
The most common cause of irreversible damage to polyamide RO
membranes is:
a. Exposure to free chlorine or strong oxidants
b. Low pH cleaning
c. Low temperature
d. Flow variations
Back: Answer: a. Exposure to free chlorine or strong oxidants

Front:
Antiscalant is added to RO feedwater to:
a. Inhibit precipitation of sparingly soluble salts
b. Increase pH
c. Disinfect the membranes
d. Remove turbidity
Back: Answer: a. Inhibit precipitation of sparingly soluble salts

Front:
SDI greater than 5 at 15 minutes usually indicates:
a. High fouling potential and need for improved pretreatment
b. Membrane oxidation
c. Adequate pretreatment
d. Low hardness
Back: Answer: a. High fouling potential and need for improved pretreatment

Front:
Normalized permeate flow is used to:
pressure changes
a. Compare performance over time independent of temperature and
b. Measure instantaneous pressure only
c. Replace differential pressure monitoring
d. Measure turbidity
Back: Answer: a. Compare performance over time independent of temperature and

Front:
A sudden drop in RO permeate flow with stable differential pressure
may indicate:
a. Feed valve closure or pump malfunction
b. Biofouling
c. Membrane oxidation
d. Increased SDI
Back: Answer: a. Feed valve closure or pump malfunction

Front:
A low pH cleaning solution for RO membranes is used mainly to:
a. Dissolve inorganic scales such as calcium carbonate
b. Remove biofilm only
c. Increase salt rejection temporarily
d. Remove free chlorine
Back: Answer: a. Dissolve inorganic scales such as calcium carbonate

Front:
A high pH cleaning solution for RO membranes is used mainly to:
a. Remove organic and biological foulants
b. Remove silica scale only
c. Lower alkalinity
d. Remove iron scale only
Back: Answer: a. Remove organic and biological foulants

Front:
Scaling in the tail-end RO elements is often indicated by:
permeate flow
a. Increased differential pressure and reduced tail-element
b. Decreased permeate conductivity
c. Low feed pH
d. Higher UVT
Back: Answer: a. Increased differential pressure and reduced tail-element

Front:
Permeate conductivity increasing gradually over months usually
means:
a. Gradual membrane aging or damage
b. Instrument calibration error only
c. Lower feed conductivity
d. Lower recovery
Back: Answer: a. Gradual membrane aging or damage

Front:
RO feed pumps are typically controlled to maintain:
a. A target feed pressure or flow to achieve design recovery
b. Constant motor speed in all cases
c. Only suction pressure
d. Only concentrate flow
Back: Answer: a. A target feed pressure or flow to achieve design recovery

Front:
Energy recovery devices in RO systems are used to:
a. Recover hydraulic energy from the concentrate stream
b. Increase differential pressure across membranes
c. Reduce flux
d. Increase chlorine residual
Back: Answer: a. Recover hydraulic energy from the concentrate stream

Front:
High recovery in RO systems tends to:
a. Increase scaling tendency and concentrate TDS
b. Reduce scaling tendency
c. Eliminate need for antiscalant
d. Have no impact on concentrate quality
Back: Answer: a. Increase scaling tendency and concentrate TDS

Front:
A typical first response to fouling in an RO skid is:
cleaning
a. Verify instruments and then schedule appropriate chemical
b. Increase feed pressure indefinitely
c. Double the recovery
d. Turn off pretreatment
Back: Answer: a. Verify instruments and then schedule appropriate chemical

Front:
A permeate backpressure can:
a. Reduce driving force and lower permeate flow
b. Increase flux
c. Reduce differential pressure
d. Improve salt passage
Back: Answer: a. Reduce driving force and lower permeate flow

Front:
RO ΔP increases but permeate conductivity remains constant. What
does this indicate?
a. Membrane breach
b. Hydraulic fouling (particulate/biofouling)
c. Analyzer drift
d. Chemical scaling
Back: Answer: b. Hydraulic fouling (particulate/biofouling)

Front:
RO permeate conductivity increases but ΔP is stable. Which is true?
a. Fouling
b. Membrane salt rejection loss
c. Scaling
d. Air entrainment
Back: Answer: b. Membrane salt rejection loss

Front:
RO stage-by-stage flows show high lead-stage permeate and very low
tail-stage permeate. Cause?
a. O-ring leak
b. Analyzer drift
c. Tail-stage fouling or scaling
d. Air entrainment
Back: Answer: c. Tail-stage fouling or scaling

Front:
RO feed ORP suddenly drops. Why?
a. Analyzer malfunction
b. Excess bisulfite feed
c. UVT increased
d. pH decreased
Back: Answer: b. Excess bisulfite feed

Front:
RO NDP decreases even though feed TDS increases. Why?
a. Membrane fouling
b. Higher temperature reduces viscosity
c. Lower recovery
d. Analyzer drift
Back: Answer: b. Higher temperature reduces viscosity

Front:
RO feed SDI increases steadily. Which upstream process is most
likely underperforming?
a. UV
b. MF/UF
c. RO concentrate tank
d. Permeate pump
Back: Answer: b. MF/UF

Front:
RO lead-element permeate flow drops while tail-element flow stays
normal. Explanation?
a. Lead-element fouling or scaling
b. Tail-element fouling
c. O-ring failure
d. Analyzer drift
Back: Answer: a. Lead-element fouling or scaling

Front:
RO ΔP decreases unexpectedly while flows remain constant. Cause?
a. Scaling
b. Fouling
c. Temperature increase reducing viscosity
d. Analyzer failure
Back: Answer: c. Temperature increase reducing viscosity

Front:
Permeate conductivity decreases while feed conductivity is stable.
Most likely:
a. Analyzer error
b. Lower temperature improving salt rejection
c. Membrane damage
d. O-ring leak
Back: Answer: b. Lower temperature improving salt rejection

Front:
RO concentrate flow increases without change in feed flow. Which is
true?
a. Recovery has decreased
b. Recovery has increased
c. Feed pressure has dropped
d. Lead-element fouling occurred
Back: Answer: a. Recovery has decreased

Front:
Normalized permeate flow is decreasing while normalized salt passage
is constant. Interpretation?
a. Fouling or compaction
b. Scaling
c. Membrane breach
d. Analyzer drift
Back: Answer: a. Fouling or compaction

Front:
RO tail element pressure increases more rapidly than lead elements.
Most likely:
a. Biofouling in lead stage
b. Colloidal or particulate fouling in tail stage
c. Oxidation of membranes
d. Low pH
Back: Answer: b. Colloidal or particulate fouling in tail stage

Front:
RO feed ORP rises unexpectedly even though bisulfite dosing is
stable. Cause?
a. Bisulfite pump losing prime or injection failure
b. High temperature
c. Low pH
d. Analyzer drift
Back: Answer: a. Bisulfite pump losing prime or injection failure

Front:
RO system experiences permeate conductivity drift upward but ΔP
remains normal. Cause?
a. Gradual loss of salt rejection
b. Colloidal fouling
c. Air entrainment
d. Analyzer turbidity error
Back: Answer: a. Gradual loss of salt rejection

Front:
RO feed pump cavitation is most likely due to:
a. High feed pressure
b. Membrane fouling
c. Low net positive suction head (NPSHa)
d. High temperature
Back: Answer: c. Low net positive suction head (NPSHa)

Front:
RO concentrate flow suddenly drops with stable feed flow. Most
likely cause:
a. Scaling
b. Concentrate valve partially closed or drifting
c. Analyzer error
d. High UVT
Back: Answer: b. Concentrate valve partially closed or drifting

Front:
Lead-stage ΔP is stable, tail-stage ΔP is increasing, and permeate
conductivity is unchanged. This pattern indicates:
a. Biofouling in lead elements
b. Colloidal/particulate fouling in tail stage
c. Membrane oxidation
d. Undersized concentrate valve
Back: Answer: b. Colloidal/particulate fouling in tail stage

Front:
Scaling persists in the RO tail despite correct antiscalant dose.

mixing)

Front:
Permeate conductivity slowly increases while ΔP and flows remain
stable. What is the most likely cause?
a. Gradual loss of salt rejection (membrane aging/oxidation)
b. Colloidal fouling in the tail
c. VFD/pump mechanical issues
d. Flow meter drift
Back: Answer: a. Gradual loss of salt rejection (membrane aging/oxidation)

Front:
Net driving pressure (NDP) increases significantly, but feed
conductivity and temperature remain constant. Which is most likely?
pressure
a. Osmotic pressure increased
b. Fouling increased hydraulic resistance, requiring higher feed
c. Permeate pressure dropped to zero
d. Membranes compacted due to chemical cleaning
Back: Answer: b. Fouling increased hydraulic resistance, requiring higher feed

Front:
An RO system shows both increasing ΔP and rising permeate
conductivity. What cleaning sequence is most appropriate?
a. Caustic/surfactant cleaning followed by acid cleaning
b. Acid cleaning only
c. High-pH cleaning only
d. Sodium bisulfite flush only
Back: Answer: a. Caustic/surfactant cleaning followed by acid cleaning

Front:
RO feed conductivity increases while permeate conductivity stays
stable. This indicates:
a. Osmotic pressure increase
b. Membrane breach
c. Scaling in tail elements
d. Flow meter drift
Back: Answer: a. Osmotic pressure increase

Front:
RO normalized permeate flow is decreasing but ΔP is stable. Cause?
a. Loss of membrane permeability (fouling/compaction)
b. Scaling
c. Analyzer failure
d. Air entrainment
Back: Answer: a. Loss of membrane permeability (fouling/compaction)

Front:
Tail-stage permeate flow decreases while lead-stage remains
constant. Most likely:
a. Biofouling in lead stage
b. Scaling/fouling in tail stage
c. Pump cavitation
d. Valve malfunction
Back: Answer: b. Scaling/fouling in tail stage

Front:
RO permeate pH slowly increases over weeks. Which scenario fits?
a. CO₂ stripping in permeate tank
b. Weak-base amines passing through membranes
c. Antiscalant overdose
d. Caustic feed pump failure
Back: Answer: b. Weak-base amines passing through membranes

Front:
During startup, RO feed pressure spikes and permeate flow stalls.
Cause?
a. High temperature
b. High recovery
c. Trapped air in pressure vessel
d. High pH
Back: Answer: c. Trapped air in pressure vessel

Front:
Sudden drop in RO feed ORP despite stable bisulfite dosing.
Explanation?
a. Bisulfite line plugging or pump failure
b. High pH
c. Scaling
d. Membrane oxidation
Back: Answer: a. Bisulfite line plugging or pump failure

Front:
A gradual increase in RO transmembrane pressure (TMP) while permeate
quality remains stable most likely indicates:
a. Organic fouling on the membrane surface
b. Membrane integrity failure
c. Increased feed salinity
d. Permeate backpressure
Back: Answer: a. Organic fouling on the membrane surface

Front:
A sudden increase in RO feed pressure while maintaining constant
recovery most likely indicates:
a. Increased membrane fouling requiring higher operating pressure
b. Scaling in the tail elements only
c. Membrane compaction
d. Insufficient antiscalant dosage
Back: Answer: a. Increased membrane fouling requiring higher operating pressure

Front:
Which condition most promotes calcium carbonate scaling in RO
concentrate?
a. Increasing pH in the concentrate stream
b. Low alkalinity in the feed
c. High temperature in the feedwater
d. Decreasing recovery
Back: Answer: a. Increasing pH in the concentrate stream

Front:
A rapid decline in permeate quality (higher TDS) without a change in
TMP most likely indicates:
a. Membrane damage or loss of salt rejection
b. Biological fouling
c. Low temperature
d. Reduced antiscalant feed
Back: Answer: a. Membrane damage or loss of salt rejection

Front:
Normalized permeate flow is used to:
temperature and pressure changes

Back: Answer: a. Compare membrane performance over time independent of

Increased concentration polarization at the membrane surface results
in:

d. Improved salt rejection
Back: Answer: a. Higher osmotic pressure and reduced permeate flux

Front:
A differential pressure increase only in the first RO stage most

lead elements

Front:
Which parameter has the strongest direct effect on osmotic pressure?
a. Feedwater TDS concentration
b. Temperature
c. Total hardness
d. pH
Back: Answer: a. Feedwater TDS concentration

Front:
The primary reason RO membranes undergo clean-in-place (CIP) is to:
a. Remove accumulated foulants and restore flux and performance
b. Reduce permeate salinity permanently
c. Increase silica solubility
d. Improve UVT for downstream UV AOP
Back: Answer: a. Remove accumulated foulants and restore flux and performance

Front:
Which foulant is best removed using acid-based cleaning? *a. Calcium
carbonate scale
b. Biological slime
c. Organic fouling
d. Silica polymerization
Back: Answer: (not marked)

Front:
Membrane compaction is most likely to occur when:
a. Operating at high pressures for extended periods
b. Recovery is too low
c. Permeate backpressure is reduced
d. Feedwater temperature increases
Back: Answer: a. Operating at high pressures for extended periods

Front:
What effect does elevated feedwater temperature have on RO
operation?
a. Increases permeate flux due to lower viscosity
b. Decreases permeate flux because membranes contract
c. Increases scaling potential
d. Decreases salt passage
Back: Answer: a. Increases permeate flux due to lower viscosity

Front:
The purpose of a concentrate control valve in RO operation is to:
flow
a. Maintain the desired system recovery by regulating concentrate
b. Control permeate TDS
c. Increase feed pH
d. Remove dissolved gases
Back: Answer: a. Maintain the desired system recovery by regulating concentrate

Front:
A sudden drop in RO permeate pH while feed pH remains unchanged
suggests:
a. Membrane degradation allowing passage of acidic species
b. CO₂ stripping in the feed tank
c. Antiscalant overdose
d. Low recovery
Back: Answer: a. Membrane degradation allowing passage of acidic species

Front:
Concentrate recirculation is sometimes used to:
a. Improve system recovery without exceeding scaling limits
b. Reduce feed temperature
c. Improve permeate salinity
d. Reduce TMP
Back: Answer: a. Improve system recovery without exceeding scaling limits

Front:
In RO pretreatment, the most effective method to prevent colloidal
fouling is:
a. Reducing SDI (Silt Density Index) below acceptable limits
b. Adding sodium hypochlorite upstream
c. Lowering alkalinity
d. Operating at high pH
Back: Answer: a. Reducing SDI (Silt Density Index) below acceptable limits

Front:
Which phenomenon increases salt passage at constant TMP?
a. Membrane oxidation or damage
b. Improved mass transfer
c. Reduced concentration polarization
d. Increased feed temperature
Back: Answer: a. Membrane oxidation or damage

Front:
High permeate backpressure in RO results in:
a. Reduced permeate flux and potential membrane damage
b. Increased recovery
c. Decreased scaling potential
d. Lower salt passage
Back: Answer: a. Reduced permeate flux and potential membrane damage

Front:
Silica fouling is most likely to occur when:
design
a. Silica concentration is high and recovery increases beyond
b. pH is very low
c. Temperature decreases
d. Chlorine residual is high
Back: Answer: a. Silica concentration is high and recovery increases beyond

Front:
What is the primary effect of scaling on RO performance?
a. Increased TMP and reduced permeate flow
b. Reduced salt passage
c. Increased recovery
d. Improved flux stability
Back: Answer: a. Increased TMP and reduced permeate flow

Front:
In RO, which cleaning chemical is most appropriate for removing
calcium carbonate scale?
a. Sodium hydroxide.
b. Surfactant solution.
c. Acid solution (e.g., citric or hydrochloric acid).
d. Sodium hypochlorite.
Back: Answer: c. Acid solution (e.g., citric or hydrochloric acid).

Front:
An RO system operates at a design flux of 15 GFD (gallons per square
foot per day). If the total membrane area is 40,000 ft² and the
recovery is 80%, what is the total permeate flow rate in GPM?
a. 417 GPM
b. 333 GPM
c. 521 GPM
d. 600 GPM
Back: Answer: a. 417 GPM

Front:
A Reverse Osmosis (RO) system is experiencing a rapid and sustained
increase in TMP while permeate quality remains high and feed pH is
unchanged. What is the most likely cause?
a. Membrane integrity loss due to a tear or hole.
b. Irreversible organic fouling on the membrane surface.
c. A significant increase in feedwater temperature.
d. Failure of the antiscalant chemical feed pump.
Back: Answer: b. Irreversible organic fouling on the membrane surface.

Front:
In an operating RO system, the salt passage is 5%. If the feedwater
TDS is 1000 mg/L, what is the expected permeate TDS?
a. 5 mg/L
b. 50 mg/L
c. 95 mg/L
d. 100 mg/L
Back: Answer: b. 50 mg/L

Front:
In RO operations, which parameter is most directly affected by
changes in feedwater temperature?
a. Permeate TDS
b. Membrane surface charge
c. Permeate flux
d. Concentrate pH
Back: Answer: c. Permeate flux

Front:
What is the most likely cause of a sudden drop in RO permeate
quality without a corresponding change in TMP?
a. Organic fouling on the membrane surface
b. Membrane damage leading to compromised salt rejection
c. Reduced antiscalant dosing
d. Decrease in feed flow rate
Back: Answer: b. Membrane damage leading to compromised salt rejection

Front:
A plant observes an increase in differential pressure only in the RO
lead stage. What is the most likely cause?
first stage
a. Scaling occurring in the tail elements
b. Accumulation of suspended solids or biological growth in the

Which statement best describes the role of the concentrate
minimization step in an AWT facility?
further treatment.

Back: Answer: b. It reduces the volume of RO concentrate requiring disposal or

Front:
A decrease in RO permeate flow together with an increase in salt
passage most likely indicates:
a. Organic fouling only
b. Scaling only
c. Membrane compaction or irreversible degradation
d. A failure in the concentrate control valve
Back: Answer: c. Membrane compaction or irreversible degradation

Front:
Which condition most strongly promotes calcium carbonate scaling in
RO systems?
a. Low feedwater alkalinity
b. Decreasing feedwater pH
c. Increasing pH in the concentrate stream
d. Higher feed temperature
Back: Answer: c. Increasing pH in the concentrate stream

Front:
During operation of an RO system, permeate backpressure increases
significantly. What is the expected effect?
a. Increases permeate flux
b. Decreases permeate flux and may damage membranes
c. Decreases concentrate pressure
d. Eliminates antiscalant requirements
Back: Answer: b. Decreases permeate flux and may damage membranes

Front:
In RO concentrate management, which method is considered a
volume-reduction technology rather than a disposal method?
a. Deep-well injection
b. Ocean discharge under NPDES permit
c. Brine concentrators or evaporators
d. Land application for irrigation
Back: Answer: c. Brine concentrators or evaporators

Front:
When operating an RO system, which factor most strongly influences
scaling potential in the concentrate stream?
a. Membrane age
b. Permeate recovery rate
c. Concentration factor of sparingly soluble ions
d. Temperature correction factor (TCF)
Back: Answer: c. Concentration factor of sparingly soluble ions

Front:
What is the primary operational purpose of conducting a
clean-in-place (CIP) on an RO system?
a. To restore RO permeate salinity to its theoretical minimum
b. To remove accumulated foulants and restore flux and efficiency
c. To reduce antiscalant demand
d. To disinfect downstream pipelines
Back: Answer: b. To remove accumulated foulants and restore flux and efficiency

Front:
In RO pretreatment, which method is most effective at preventing
biological fouling of membranes?
a. Increasing pH above 9.0
b. Using high-dose polymeric coagulant
c. Maintaining a consistent disinfectant residual upstream of MF/UF
d. Reducing feed temperature
Back: Answer: c. Maintaining a consistent disinfectant residual upstream of MF/UF

Front:
In UV AOP systems, an RO–UV train often shows increased UVT after
RO. What is the primary reason?
a. RO increases the concentration of NOM
b. MF removes all dissolved organics
c. RO removes DOC and chromophores that absorb UV light
d. UVT is independent of dissolved organic matter
Back: Answer: c. RO removes DOC and chromophores that absorb UV light

Front:
In RO systems, which operational parameter is most directly
influenced by feed TDS?
a. pH
b. Temperature
c. Osmotic pressure
d. Alkalinity
Back: Answer: c. Osmotic pressure

Front:
A plant observes that RO recovery has dropped while TMP remains
stable. What is the most likely cause?
a. Organic fouling
b. Scaling on the concentrate side
c. Permeate flow control valve restriction or instrumentation error
d. Sudden increase in feed salinity
Back: Answer: c. Permeate flow control valve restriction or instrumentation error

Front:
In RO systems, elevated feedwater temperature generally:
a. Increases permeate TDS
b. Increases permeate flux due to lower viscosity
c. Increases scaling tendency
d. Increases membrane compaction
Back: Answer: b. Increases permeate flux due to lower viscosity

Front:
Which operational condition most contributes to colloidal fouling in
RO systems?
a. High feed temperature
b. High silt density index (SDI) in the pretreatment filtrate
c. Low alkalinity
d. Low recovery operation
Back: Answer: b. High silt density index (SDI) in the pretreatment filtrate

Front:
A sudden increase in RO feed pressure while maintaining constant
recovery most likely indicates:
a. Scaling in the tail elements
b. Increased membrane fouling requiring higher operating pressure
c. Membrane compaction
d. Reduced concentrate backpressure
Back: Answer: b. Increased membrane fouling requiring higher operating pressure

Front:
A utility observes an unexpected increase in permeate conductivity

a. Scaling in the concentrate stage
b. Membrane surface damage or loss of rejection
c. Low temperature reducing flux

Back: Answer: b. Membrane surface damage or loss of rejection

Front:
Which cleaning chemistry is most appropriate for removing organic
biofouling?
a. Citric acid
b. Hydrochloric acid
c. High-pH cleaners with surfactants
d. Sodium bisulfite
Back: Answer: c. High-pH cleaners with surfactants

Front:
What is the primary reason to maintain minimum velocity in RO feed
channels?
a. To reduce permeate TDS
b. To minimize particulate settling and biofilm formation
c. To increase osmotic pressure
d. To reduce energy consumption
Back: Answer: b. To minimize particulate settling and biofilm formation

Front:
In an MF–RO–UV AOP treatment train, which barrier provides the
greatest removal of dissolved inorganic constituents?
a. UV AOP
b. GAC adsorption
c. Reverse Osmosis (RO)
d. Microfiltration (MF)
Back: Answer: c. Reverse Osmosis (RO)

Front:
In an MF–RO–UV AOP train, the primary pathogen removal barrier is:
a. MF
b. UV AOP
c. RO
d. GAC
Back: Answer: c. RO

Front:
In RO operations, which condition most increases the potential for
silica scaling?
a. Low feed temperature
b. High pH in the feed stream
c. High silica concentration combined with high recovery
d. High free chlorine residual
Back: Answer: c. High silica concentration combined with high recovery

Front:
RO energy consumption is most directly influenced by:
a. Permeate temperature
b. Feed pressure required to overcome osmotic pressure
c. Free chlorine concentration
d. Permeate pH
Back: Answer: b. Feed pressure required to overcome osmotic pressure

Front:
A potable reuse system uses RO followed by UV AOP. Which parameter
must be minimized to ensure efficient hydroxyl radical generation?
a. Dissolved oxygen.
b. Hardness.
c. Radical scavengers such as bicarbonate and carbonate.
d. Silica concentration.
Back: Answer: c. Radical scavengers such as bicarbonate and carbonate.

Front:
In RO operations, normalized permeate flow (NPF) is used to:
temperature and pressure changes.
a. Measure membrane compaction only.
b. Track changes in salt passage.
c. Compare membrane performance over time independent of
d. Control chloramine dose automatically.
Back: Answer: c. Compare membrane performance over time independent of

Front:
What is the primary purpose of decarbonation after RO treatment?
a. Increase corrosion control.
b. Strip dissolved CO₂ to increase permeate pH and stabilize water.
c. Reduce nitrate concentration.
d. Improve UVT for downstream UV disinfection.
Back: Answer: b. Strip dissolved CO₂ to increase permeate pH and stabilize water.

Front:
In RO systems, which factor most increases energy demand?
a. High-temperature feedwater.
b. Increased osmotic pressure due to higher feed TDS.
c. Reduced concentrate flow.
d. Lower feed pH.
Back: Answer: b. Increased osmotic pressure due to higher feed TDS.

Front:
In RO pretreatment, coagulation is sometimes used to:
a. Increase permeate flux.
b. Reduce colloidal and particulate loading on MF or UF systems.
c. Decrease TMP in RO.
d. Prevent membrane compaction.
Back: Answer: b. Reduce colloidal and particulate loading on MF or UF systems.
